chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Talha ibn Zayd, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying:
The reporters of the Book are many, but its due carers are few; and how many a seeker of advice from the hadith is yet treacherous toward the Book.
The scholars are grieved by the neglect of due care, while the ignorant are grieved by the preservation of narrations.
Thus one shepherd tends its life, and another shepherd tends its destruction. At that point the two shepherds diverge and the two groups part ways.

key_terms.الرِّعَايَةِ: Due care — conscientious embodiment and practice of the Book's teachings
key_terms.رُعَاتَهُ: Its due carers/guardians — those who embody and protect the spirit and guidance of the Book
key_terms.رُوَاةَ الْكِتَابِ: Reporters/narrators of the Book — those who transmit hadith and the Quran textually
key_terms.مُسْتَغِشٍّ لِلْكِتَابِ: One treacherous toward the Book — inwardly unfaithful to the Quran's real guidance
key_terms.مُسْتَنْصِحٍ لِلْحَدِيثِ: One who seeks advice from hadith — the outwardly pious who rely on narrations

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about the difference between narrators of hadith and true guardians of the Quran?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) draws a sharp contrast between those who merely transmit hadith (narrators) and those who truly embody and guard the Book (Quran). He uses the metaphor of two shepherds — one who preserves the flock and one who leads it to ruin — to describe the scholars grieved by neglect and the ignorant grieved by diligent transmission. This narration was transmitted through Talha ibn Zayd, a Sunni narrator, indicating the universality of this warning. The Imam's audience would have recognized the tension between memorization-as-virtue and genuine understanding of the Quran's guidance.
